entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Drawing on material culture, primary sources, and wider overviews, this course delves into the time period from 100 BC to 350 AD.

This topic is included in the following course(s): History: Grades 10-12 (U.S.), History: Grade 10 (Canada), History: Grades 11-12 (Canada)

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Inquisitive 9th graders could enjoy this course, but the main texts have an advanced reading level, so students would likely want to move at a slower pace.

blocks.text:
• Take a second to recall what you read previously in the same book or topic.

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Read the selection assigned OR read for the number of minutes allocated, leaving time for narration and mapwork. Use whichever guide (i.e., pages or minutes) works best for you. You want to read enough to be interesting, but not so much that you feel overwhelmed.

• If a book is challenging for you as a student, try stopping to narrate to yourself silently for a minute every now and then to make sure you are tracking. You might also want to read aloud to yourself. Or you might want to listen to an audiobook version of the text and read along with it. 

• If a book is an easy read, enjoy the ride! 

• Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your commonplace book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

• Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. 

• To keep yourself on track, you might want to set a timer, so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

• After your narration, think about how what you read connects to other subjects, other books, and other things you've read, watched, or seen in the past or present. 

• Share any ideas that are particularly interesting to you with your fellow classmates, teachers, parents, friends, or others. You might even want to do a bit more reading or research on something on your own time in the afternoon or evenings.

These lessons are written directly to the student, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. Accountability components are added to facilitate teacher/student discussion and growing independence. 

Those educating at home might pick one or two history lessons to read aloud with their students to keep up the habit of oral narration and foster conversation and relationship, and then simply give students these lesson plans and the rest of the books and check in with them throughout the term for conversation, support, and accountability. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons that students complete themselves silently and others read aloud and narrated together. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons, after everyone has narrated either together or independently in writing.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Welcome to the Empire
⍞ Materials: Ancient Empires

➜ INTRO 
What comes to your mind when you hear the word "empire?" Historians disagree on many things including times and dates, translations, and terminology. One of the terms that is debated is the word "empire" and its meaning. As you read through the introduction to Ancient Empires, what definition do you agree with? Why do you agree with it? You're invited to answer these questions aloud or write them down.

➜ ANNOTATE
Ancient Empires is a non-fiction book which makes it a good candidate for annotation. While you are reading through the text you may encounter an interesting point or main idea that you want to underline. You could put a question mark next to a statement you find unclear. You may place sticky notes on a page that you want to return too. Experiment with different ways to engage with the information in the book. Some students will record themselves reading or talking about the reading. Others may start a discussion with an acquaintance about the material. Try different ways and see what works and what doesn’t work for you. You can discuss your findings with your teacher.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Introduction: "What is an (Ancient) Empire?" p.1-9 
If you have already read this resource, just review the Introduction section assigned here.

➜ WRITE
Explain the IEMP model and its importance in 1-2 paragraphs.

lessons.title: 40m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
The Late Republic
⍞ Materials: Ancient Empires

➜ INTRO
Rome had been founded in 753 BC and it became a Republic in 509 BC. The Roman Republic had been involved in many wars. The most famous of these wars are known as the three Punic Wars. The Third Punic War was fought around 149-146 BC. During the Third Punic War, Rome would clash with a sovereign territory known as Carthage and ultimately would raze it to the ground. Rome would kill most of it's male inhabitants and sell it's women and children into slavery. With the defeat of Carthage, it would seem that Roman power was complete as no other nation could stand in the way of it's expansion.
However, the Roman Republic had internal issues. It's politcal and military leaders were corrupt and despite it's incredible growth, the Republic found itself in trouble. These political and military leaders were grasping for more power afforded them by their Republic governmental system. There were also internal struggles from people groups who refused to adapt to life under their new conquerors.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ 
Ch.9 p.210-214 start at “the Late Republic” and stop at "Spartacus in 74-71 B.C."

➜ VIEW
∞ Video Link: From Enslavement to Rebel Gladiator: The Life of Spartacus

➜ NARRATE
Make a list of the main points of the reading and video, along with 1-2 paragraphs of what you found most interesting.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
How do Christians Read Classics?
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics
 
➜ INTRO
Can Christians read Greco-Roman pagan literature for spiritual formation? This is the question that Nadya Williams asks in the introduction of her book. As you read through the book, think through the above question. Do you agree with her? Why or why not?
 
➜ ANNOTATE
Christians Reading Classics is a non-fiction book which makes it a good candidate for annotation. While you are reading through the text you may encounter an interesting point or main idea that you want to underline. You could put a question mark next to a statement you find unclear. You may place sticky notes on a page that you want to return too. Experiment with different ways to engage with the information in the book. Some students will record themselves reading or talking about the reading. Others may start a discussion with an acquaintance about the material. Try different ways and see what works and what doesn’t work for you. You can discuss your findings with your teacher.
 
➜ READ & NARRATE
Introduction: p.xi-xx
∞ Link: Interview with Nadya Williams 
 
➜ WRITE
Do you think that Christians can read Greco-Roman pagan literature for spiritual formation? Are writings such as Homer, Boethius, Virgil or other ancient pagan writers spiritually beneficial for believers? Why or why not?
 
➜ PONDER
What in the Interview with Nadya Williams stands out to you?
lessons.teacherNotes: ∞ Link: Interview with Nadya Williams

lessons.title: 40m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 26
lessons.body:
Learning from Plato and Aristotle 
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics

➜ INTRO
Even though Plato and Aristotle lived during the time of the Greek empire, their influence in Roman culture can not be understated. These two men have influenced both ancient world thinking and modern day thinking about truth, virtue, the beginning of life, and other subjects. The apostles, early church fathers and mothers and later christian writers would all contend with Platonic and Aristotelian thought in their writings. As you read through this chapter, think about the amount of  influence these two men had and why it's so important for Christians to read their works. 

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Ch.8 p.101-113

➜ WRITE & DISCUSS
In three paragraphs, answer the three reflection questions located on p. 113 of the reading. Discuss your answers.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 29
lessons.body:
How to Do Anything in the Ancient World
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics

➜ INTRO
Have you ever tried to put together a piece of furniture? Or needed to fix something around the house? How did you go about completing the task? Perhaps, you might use a manual or a handbook that is provided either in paper or online. The ancient world also had manuals and handbooks that would help them survive and thrive in their time. As you read through this chapter, think about the difference between a modern day manual and an ancient manual and why it's important for Christians to read these works.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Ch.10 p.129-133 end at "do no harm" 

➜ PONDER
How should Christians go about reading ancient handbooks and manuals?
lessons.teacherNotes:
• COMPOSITION
Write a 2-3 page manual of your own.

Cicero, Caesar, and Political Rhetoric in the Roman Republic
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics

➜ INTRO
The political sphere of the Roman Empire is a cut-throat business. So much so, that if one person was elected, their life might be immediately in danger as their opponent may plot an assassination for the winning man. Such is the case of Cicero. As you'll be able to see in the reading, these documents tell us so much more than just an assassination attempt.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 37
lessons.body:
Cato and Livy in The Roman Republic
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics
 
➜ INTRO
Nadya Williams writes, "Homer's epics and Herodotus's histories celebrated heroes. But this is not Sparta; this is Rome. The heroes here are Romans first--or, at least, so Cato dreamed. In the end, his approach to writing history didn't become an example that anyone else followed. And yet the broader goal of Cato's history--to make virtuous Roman men and women by showing them examples of the virtues to imitate--continued. Rome's historians deliberately wrote exemplary histories."

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Ch.13 p.171-178 end at "you are men."

 ➜ WRITE

Marcus Aurelius
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics

➜ INTRO
People in the Roman Empire were asking important questions about humanity, truth, virtue and soul. Nadya Williams writes, "What is the nature of the soul dwelling within each human body? And what is the relationship of the soul to the body? The pre-Christian Greeks and Romans thought much about these questions, even though their answers ran up against the limits of pagan theology. Nevertheless, many of them were firmly convinced that a soul—some sort of intangible spiritual portion—inhabited the physical body." Apuleius and Marcus Aurelius would consider the soul in their writings. As you read through this chapter, think about how Christians should read these works.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 53
lessons.body:
Introduction to Early Church Writings and Clement
⍞ Materials: Early Christian Writings
 
➜ INTRO
Imagine uncovering the writing of an Early Church Father as you sift through a monastic library in the East, or as you begin to use that writing as a wrapping paper for raw fish and seafood. That is the reality of some of these texts translated in this collection of Early Christian Writers. 
These texts offer the modern-day reader more than early church doctrine and theology; they also offer us insights into the issues that the early church was facing as it began to follow the teachings of Christ. 

➜ NOTE
The first and second century Christians are operating in a world wholly different than our own. They are operating in empires that have different values, virtues, and myths. Moreover, these people are trying to figure out Jesus, his relationship to God and the connection of the Holy Spirit and they are operating with the Septuagint (The Greek Translation of the Hebrew Bible), the Gospels and some of the letters. Keep in mind that the canon of the Bible will not be official until late fourth century. 
As you read through these texts, take a moment to put your modern day theological and biblical knowledge to the side. Listen to the words of these Christians. What are they asking? What are they teaching? Why might these be the questions that they are taking the time to answer? All of these questions can help us understand the early church world better and see where these early church writers are taking inspiration from.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.
 
➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

Clement's Letters and Intro to Ignatius
⍞ Materials: Early Christian Writings
 
➜ INTRO
There are many ways to measure the success of an emperor. One way is to measure the size of the nation that they ruled. It was under Emperor Trajan's rule that the Roman Empire would reach its pinnacle in terms of territory. 
But under his rule, Trajan would also persecute Christians. One such martyr would be Ignatius of Antioch, who was the third Bishop of Antioch after Peter. Ignatius would write a series of letters to cities under his leadership, guiding them with doctrinal and practical practices that would help them live out their Christian faith. 
 
➜ NOTE
As you read through these texts, take a moment to put your modern day theological and biblical knowledge to the side. Listen to the words of these Christians. What are they asking? terms.content:
· In what ways does the Roman Republic remind you of your own country? In what ways is it different?

· Draw two pieces of art that you remember seeing this term. Briefly say what they are and describe them. What do you think they say about the cultures that they were a part of?

· Choose Cicero, Caesar, Tacitus, Perpetua, Suetonius, or Marcus Aurelius, and explore how their writings can influence the modern day church today.

· How should Christians go about reading pagan classics? How can reading these classics benefit spiritual formation?

· Early Christian Writings: Based on the writings of the early church fathers that you have read this term, what were some of the primary concerns of the early church? What are the most common themes? Are the concerns of the early church the same as or different than the concerns of the Christian church today?

· Summarize one letter of your choosing. Then share how that letter gives us insight into the life of early Christians in the Roman Empire.
